strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically motivated problem: training a policy purely offline from delay-free data and deploying it in a delayed environment, which sits at the intersection of offline RL and delayed RL. The authors make a credible case that no prior work learns delay-robust policies solely from delay-free data.

The core idea is clean and well-motivated: embedding a transformer-based belief predictor inside a behavior-regularized policy-iteration loop (rather than a frozen two-stage pipeline or raw state augmentation), with an explicit argument for why the two-stage alternative fails (biased value targets, distribution mismatch, sample inefficiency).

The empirical evaluation is broad: 3 environments x 4 D4RL dataset types x 3 delay lengths x 2 delay regimes (deterministic and stochastic), covering 36 task-delay combinations per table, with a consistent trend favoring the method and gaps that widen with delay length as theory would predict.
The method has a modular, reproducible design (transformer belief + BRAC/TD3+BC-style regularization + n-step returns), and hyperparameters and code are provided in the supplementary material.
Limitations are acknowledged honestly in the conclusion (known deterministic delay, locomotion-only scope, offline sample-complexity analysis left open).
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is thin. Lemmas 4.1 and 4.2 are imported from prior work [49], Proposition 4.3 is a straightforward policy-improvement argument, and key derivation steps in Appendix A are informal (e.g., 'with proper choice of α it is easy to unify' the Wasserstein terms) without rigorously establishing that the required constants exist or that the Lipschitz assumptions hold in practice.

All baselines are constructed by the authors (Aug-BC, Aug-CQL, Belief-CQL). There is no comparison against adapting existing delayed-RL methods (e.g., DIDA, DFBT-style belief forecasting, or D-SAC) to the offline setting, nor against running strong standard offline RL algorithms (IQL, TD3+BC) on delay-free data with a simple learned state estimator. The baseline set feels tailored.

No seeds, standard deviations, or statistical significance tests are reported; tables show single numbers for 36 configurations, which is concerning given RL variance, especially where margins are small (e.g., Belief-CQL nearly ties DT-CORL in many cells).

HalfCheetah results are weak in absolute terms (e.g., deterministic expert: 20.6 at delay 4, 5.1 at delay 8; medium: 27.8 at delay 8), yet the text emphasizes Hopper/Walker successes and does not analyze this failure mode, undermining the generality claims.

The setting assumes a known, deterministic delay length Δ, and the framework must be retrained per delay value; this limits applicability to the realistic case of unknown or time-varying latency, which is acknowledged but not addressed even empirically.
The claimed 'sim-to-real' motivation is never tested—experiments are entirely in MuJoCo simulation with synthetic delays, so the central sim-to-real narrative is asserted rather than evidenced.

Writing has multiple typos and loose phrasing ('arrive the new policy iteration framework', 'vannila', 'it is easy to unify'), and Remark 4.5 concedes that no formal sample-efficiency claim is actually proven despite efficiency being a headline contribution.

strengths: The offline-training / delayed-deployment setting is a practically relevant and relatively underexplored problem: learning delay-robust policies purely from delay-free logs is a sensible formulation, and the paper motivates it well.

The empirical evaluation covers a reasonably broad grid (3 locomotion tasks x 4 D4RL dataset types x deterministic and stochastic delays x 3 delay lengths), and the proposed method shows clear gains over augmentation-based baselines as delay length grows.
The paper is upfront about some limitations (known, fixed delay length Delta; locomotion-only tasks), and provides implementation details and hyperparameter tables in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core components are largely assembled from prior work: the lemmas in Sec. 4.1 are explicitly imported from [49] and [47] (apparently the authors' own prior line of work on belief-based delayed RL), the policy constraint follows ReBRAC/TD3+BC [37, 9], and the transformer belief follows DFBT [47]. The main new element is the integration of a (pretrained-style) belief model into a behavior-regularized offline policy iteration loop, which is an incremental combination rather than a substantive methodological advance.

The theoretical contribution is thin and loosely argued. Proposition 4.3 is a routine monotonic-improvement argument; the appendix derivation relies on hand-waving such as 'with proper choice of alpha it is easy to unify that all the 1-Wasserstein terms' without stating conditions; Remark 4.5 concedes that no formal offline sample-efficiency analysis is provided. Lemma A.1's statement and proof contain notational inconsistencies (e.g., expectations over x~D inside expressions where x is already bound).

Overclaimed framing. The abstract and conclusion repeatedly invoke 'bridging the sim-to-real latency gap' and 'real-world' deployment, but all experiments are synthetic delays injected into MuJoCo simulation. No real-robot or even non-locomotion experiment is presented, so the sim-to-real claims are unsupported.

Weak and partially unfair baselines. The baselines are custom constructs (Aug-BC, Aug-CQL, Belief-CQL) rather than established delayed-RL methods (e.g., DIDA, BPQL, VDPO adapted to the offline setting) or the obvious baseline of deploying a delay-free offline policy without any compensation. Belief-CQL actually wins a substantial number of cells (e.g., HalfCheetah medium at all stochastic delays, Hopper/Walker2d medium-replay), which the text downplays; the claim of superiority 'in 27 of 36' stochastic configurations does not hold cleanly in Table 2 as presented.

No statistical rigor: tables report single numbers with no standard deviations, number of seeds, or significance tests, despite high-variance offline RL results (e.g., HalfCheetah expert scores fluctuating from 85.1 to 5.8 across delay settings). This is a serious evaluation deficiency for a benchmark-driven paper.

No ablation studies. There is no sensitivity analysis for the regularization weights (lambda1, lambda2, alpha), no comparison of transformer belief vs. a simpler MLP/RNN belief, no ablation of the n-step returns/Retrace trick, and no analysis of belief prediction error versus task performance, making it hard to attribute the gains.

Contradictory results discussion: the text claims Belief-CQL 'becomes optimal when the delay grows longer' where it clearly means suboptimal, and the empirical narrative does not always match the tables (e.g., HalfCheetah results for DT-CORL are weak in absolute terms and deteriorate sharply with delay, contradicting the claimed uniform superiority).

Writing quality issues: inconsistent method naming (DT-CORL vs DT-CORL with en-dashes), typos ('vannila', 'arrive the final derivation', 'easily have have'), a policy defined as pi: S x A -> [0,1] without normalizing over the action simplex, and other polish problems that suggest the paper was not carefully proofread.

Practical scope is narrow: the method assumes a known, fixed (or max) delay length and trains a separate belief transformer per Delta; heterogeneous or unknown delays, which the paper itself admits, limit real-world applicability, and no strategy for delay estimation is offered.

strengths: Novel and practically motivated problem setting: learning delay-robust policies purely offline from delay-free trajectories for deployment under delayed feedback. The related-work review credibly supports the claim that no prior method addresses this offline delayed RL setting.

Clear conceptual contribution: embedding a transformer-based belief predictor inside a behavior-regularized policy-iteration loop (rather than a frozen two-stage pipeline), which the paper motivates well via three concrete failure modes (biased value targets, distribution mismatch, sample efficiency in stochastic MDPs).

Reasonable theoretical scaffolding: the paper formally connects the augmented-MDP constrained policy iteration to a belief-based formulation (Lemmas 4.1-4.2, Prop. 4.3 with proofs in the appendix), grounding the algorithmic design.

Fairly extensive empirical evaluation: 3 locomotion tasks x 4 D4RL dataset types x deterministic and stochastic delays (Δ ∈ {4,8,16}), with thoughtfully constructed baselines (Aug-BC, Aug-CQL, Belief-CQL) that isolate each design component. Results against augmentation baselines are decisive and widen with delay, supporting the core claims.
Implementation details, hyperparameters, and a codebase (based on CORL/CleanRL) are provided, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Mixed results weaken the headline claim of consistent superiority. On HalfCheetah, DT-CORL performs poorly in absolute terms (e.g., 47.4/27.8/6.4 on medium with deterministic delays) and Belief-CQL actually wins in a substantial number of cells (e.g., HalfCheetah medium 4-step stochastic: 52.6 vs 48.2; medium-replay stochastic: several cells). The abstract and Sec. 5 prose ('remarkably outperforms', 'consistently surpasses') overstate what the tables show; a more honest accounting (e.g., win-rate across all cells including HalfCheetah) is needed.

All baselines are constructed by the authors from generic components (BC, CQL, belief-CQL). No comparison against existing delayed-RL methods (DIDA, BPQL, VDPO, DFBT) adapted to the offline setting, nor against simply training on synthetically delay-augmented data — the strongest prior-art comparison is missing.

Evaluation breadth is narrow: only three MuJoCo locomotion tasks from D4RL. No anti-delay/humanoid tasks, no vision-based or manipulation settings despite the sim-to-real motivation, and no real or even simulated latency-mismatch experiment (data from a 'delay-free simulator' vs deployment dynamics differ only by injected delay).

No statistical rigor: tables report point estimates only, with no number of seeds, standard deviations, or significance tests — a significant concern given RL variance and the small margins in several comparisons.

Limited ablations: no sensitivity analysis for α (conservatism weight), transformer depth/width, the [MASK] boundary handling, n-step/Retrace choices, or belief prediction error vs. final return. The mechanism claims (e.g., 'joint belief-aware policy iteration contains this error') are asserted rather than directly measured (e.g., no belief prediction error curves).

Technical assumptions are restrictive and not fully justified: known, fixed Δ for deterministic delays (stochastic-delay handling is described but the belief model's treatment of unknown per-step lag deserves more analysis); the theory relies on Lipschitz continuity assumptions whose applicability to MuJoCo is loose; Prop. 4.3 is a fairly standard monotonic-improvement argument.

Writing and consistency issues: contradictory/typo-laden sentences (e.g., 'Belief CQL's pessimism ... becomes optimal when the delay grows longer' — presumably 'sub-optimal'), typos ('vannila', 'have have', 'effect'), inconsistent method naming, and notation sloppiness in equations (mixed μ_Δ/π_Δ terms in derivations).

The framing invokes the sim-to-real gap, but the experiments never test dynamics mismatch between the data source and the deployment environment — only injected observation delay — so the sim-to-real claim is stronger than the evidence.

strengths: Addresses a meaningful and under-explored problem: learning delay-robust policies from purely delay-free offline data, which is a realistic offline-to-online deployment scenario that existing delayed-RL and offline-RL work does not cover; the paper makes a convincing case for the practical relevance (simulators/legacy logs are delay-free while real platforms have latency).

The proposed DT-CORL framework is well-motivated: jointly training the transformer belief model with the constrained policy objective (rather than freezing a pretrained belief) directly targets the distribution-mismatch and compounding-error failure modes, and this is supported empirically by the joint-vs-separate ablation (Table 5).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple task families (D4RL AntMaze, MuJoCo locomotion with four dataset qualities, Adroit dexterous manipulation), multiple delay regimes (deterministic 4/8/16, stochastic, long 32–64 step delays, and alternative delay distributions), with sensible baseline families: augmented-state methods, naive offline RL, hybrid belief+offline-RL baselines, and an online delayed-RL SOTA method.

Useful ablations: belief architecture comparison (ensemble MLP vs. diffusion vs. transformer, with inference-speed and parameter-count trade-offs), model-capacity scaling (Table 9), and data-availability scaling (Table 4).

The paper is generally well organized, states assumptions explicitly (Lipschitz MDP/policy/Q), honestly reports settings where all methods fail (AntMaze medium-play/large-play), and acknowledges limitations (fixed known delays, open sample-complexity theory in Remark 4.5).
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: the core bounds (Lemmas 4.1/4.2, Lemma B.1) are directly imported from Wu et al. (2024b), and the derivation in B.1 mainly re-expresses the augmented-space objective in the original state space. Proposition 4.3's 'proof' in B.2 is essentially circular (it restates the definition of the argmax and asserts Bellman consistency) and does not rigorously handle the conservatism penalty; the claim that Wasserstein terms can be combined 'with the proper choice of α' is hand-wavy and the constants are never specified.

The method assumes the delay Δ is known, fixed (or treated as an effective fixed delay), and the belief model is trained for that specific Δ. This is a substantial restriction for the motivating sim-to-real scenario where latency is unknown and time-varying; the robustness experiments (Table 6) test the deployed agent under different delay distributions but do not clarify what delay the belief was trained with.

Evaluation robustness concerns: only 3 seeds per setting, which is thin for offline RL where variance across seeds is notoriously high; and the margin of superiority is small or reversed in several settings (e.g., HalfCheetah, where DT-CORL is often worse than Belief-CQL under stochastic delays and degrades sharply with delay; expert HalfCheetah drops from 85.1 to 5.8 from delay 4 to 16).

Baseline construction is somewhat favorable to the proposed method: Belief-CQL/Belief-IQL hybrids are built by the authors by feeding their own transformer belief into existing algorithms, and there is no comparison to other natural alternatives such as history-conditioned (sequence-model) policies (e.g., Decision Transformer style) acting directly on augmented observations, which is arguably the simplest competing approach for this setting.

Writing/presentation issues reduce polish: broken sentence in Sec. 5.3 ('vary the proportion ... available for training: 25'), an apparently broken/missing repository URL in the reproducibility statement ('made available in an the following repo'), several grammatical errors, and Figure 2 shows the transformer has higher final MSE (0.315) than diffusion (0.157), which is glossed over when claiming the transformer 'provides the best balance.'
No real-world or hardware experiment despite the sim-to-real latency motivation; all evaluation is simulation-only, so the central sim-to-real claim is supported only indirectly.

AntMaze results on medium-play and large-play are near zero for all methods including DT-CORL, so the framework's applicability to goal-conditioned settings is demonstrated only on the easier umaze tasks.

strengths: The problem setting is relatively underexplored: learning delay-robust policies offline from delay-free data, which the authors plausibly argue has not been directly addressed in prior delayed-RL work
The paper connects the problem to classical control ideas (Smith predictor), which is a reasonable framing

Broad empirical coverage: D4RL MuJoCo (deterministic and stochastic delays), AntMaze, Adroit hand tasks, plus ablations on belief architecture (transformer vs. ensemble MLP vs. diffusion), joint vs. separate belief training, data availability, and delay distributions
Implementation details and hyperparameters are provided in the appendix, and the authors state code will be released
weaknesses: Evaluation is statistically weak: all results use only 3 seeds with implausibly small standard deviations (e.g., 113.0 ± 0.8), which is far below the standard (5-10 seeds) for D4RL benchmarks and undermines claims of consistent superiority in an RL setting known for high variance

On the harder AntMaze tasks (medium-play, large-play), all methods including DT-CORL are near zero (0-3%), so the claimed delay-robustness advantage is only demonstrated in a narrow regime; the paper itself concedes this without analysis or remediation

The theoretical contribution is largely adapted: Lemmas 4.1/4.2 are taken directly from Wu et al. (2024b), and the appendix derivations are informal—key steps rely on hand-waving such as 'with the proper choice of α, it is easy to unify all the 1-Wasserstein terms'; Proposition 4.3's proof is a two-line argument that does not address the belief-model approximation error that is central to the method's claimed advantage

The method assumes a known, fixed (or effectively fixed) delay at deployment; the practical setting motivating the paper (unknown, time-varying latencies) is deferred to future work, weakening the sim-to-real motivation

Some experimental evidence is internally inconsistent with the narrative: Figure 2 shows the diffusion model achieves substantially lower prediction error (0.157 vs. 0.315) than the transformer, yet the text claims the transformer offers 'the best balance'—the trade-off argument needs stronger quantitative support (e.g., downstream task performance of each belief model, not just inference speed)

Baselines are constructed somewhat ad hoc by the authors (Augmented-BC, Augmented-CQL, Belief-CQL/IQL with the authors' own belief module), with hyperparameter tables for the 'Ensemble Belief' (Table 13) identical to the Transformer belief (Table 12), raising concerns about tuning fairness and copy errors in the baseline configurations

Writing quality issues persist: the code repository link is missing ('an the following repo .'), truncated text ('we vary the proportion ... 25As shown'), duplicated words ('have have'), and incorrect references (e.g., 'Thm. 4.4' when Remark 4.4 is meant)
Table 6 (delay-distribution robustness) reports only DT-CORL with no baselines, so the claimed 'strong generalization of the belief module' cannot be verified against alternatives

The deferred comparison to a formal sample-complexity analysis (Remark 4.5) is fine, but combined with the above, the paper's claims of 'essentialness' of joint belief-policy optimization rest on a limited empirical and theoretical foundation

strengths: The problem setting is genuinely interesting and relatively underexplored: learning delay-robust policies purely from delay-free offline data, motivated by the sim-to-real latency gap. The paper makes a credible case that this differs from both delayed RL (which assumes online interaction) and standard offline RL.

The framework is well-motivated: replacing state augmentation with a transformer-based belief model that is jointly trained with a policy-constrained (BRAC-style) objective, avoiding dimensional blow-up and distribution mismatch of frozen two-stage pipelines.

Broad empirical coverage: D4RL MuJoCo locomotion, AntMaze goal-conditioned tasks, Adroit dexterous manipulation, deterministic and stochastic delays up to 64 steps, multiple delay distributions, ablations on belief architecture (MLP vs. diffusion vs. transformer), model size, data availability, and joint vs. separate training.
Writing is generally clear, related work is thorough (including control-theoretic Smith predictor connections), and hyperparameters/implementation details are provided in the appendix.
The ablations (joint vs. separate belief training; transformer vs. diffusion/ensemble alternatives) directly support the paper's central design claims rather than being decorative.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is thin and partly derivative. Lemmas 4.1 and 4.2 are taken from Wu et al. (2024b), and the derivation in Appendix B.1 contains a hand-wavy step: 'with the proper choice of α, it is easy to unify all the 1-Wasserstein terms' is asserted without a precise condition or bound on the introduced constants. Proposition 4.3 (monotonic improvement) is essentially the standard BRAC-style argument applied to the regularized objective, and the proof in B.2 is incomplete (it shows improvement w.r.t. the regularized surrogate, not the true return). There are also cross-referencing errors (e.g., B.1 cites a 'Thm. 4.1' that does not exist; Proposition 4.3's proof is labeled under 'Policy Improvement').

Only 3 seeds per experiment is too few for the variance levels typical of offline RL, particularly given reported near-collapse failures of baselines (e.g., DBPT-SAC scoring 0.0 across all AntMaze cells, which suggests a possibly misconfigured baseline rather than a meaningful comparison).

Claims of consistent superiority are overstated relative to the results: DT-CORL loses to Belief-CQL on several HalfCheetah settings (e.g., medium Δ=4: 47.4 vs. 49.2; stochastic medium Δ=4: 48.2 vs. 52.6), and performance collapses on hard AntMaze tasks (medium-play and large-play are near-zero for all methods, including DT-CORL), where the paper offers no method-level solution.

A key deployment assumption is under-examined: the belief model is trained offline by inverting augmented histories to ground-truth (delay-free) states, and the method assumes the delay is known and fixed at deployment. The mismatch between the offline 'inversion' distribution and the online 'forward rollout' distribution is claimed to be handled by joint training, but no analysis or direct diagnostic measurement of belief error under deployment distribution shift is provided.

Long-delay results undermine the delay-robustness narrative: at 32–64 steps, returns drop to single digits or low teens on HalfCheetah and Hopper for all methods, and DT-CORL shows large variance (e.g., Walker2d 60.0/85.4 vs. 21.4/41.3).

Reproducibility is compromised: the reproducibility statement contains an empty repository link ('made available in an the following repo'), and the paper does not specify how the delay was injected for evaluation in enough detail to guarantee comparability with prior delayed-RL work.

Several presentation issues: inconsistent lemma/theorem numbering, the 'effectively shorter delays' argument for why belief methods benefit under stochastic delay is heuristic and not backed by analysis, and the claim of being 'the first framework' is softened by the authors' own admission of imitation-style pretraining work (Liotet et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2021) that is not empirically compared.

The connection between theory and practice is loose: the implementation uses a TD3+BC-style MSE action-matching surrogate and dataset rewards, whereas Eq. (3)–(4) involve Wasserstein terms and belief-marginalized rewards; the gap between the analyzed objective and the optimized one is not quantified.
